---
title: "Benchmarks: R8, R52, MR, Ohsumed, 20NG"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r values, include = FALSE}
results <- read.csv("benchmark-results.csv")
published <- read.csv("benchmark-published.csv")
lowlabel <- read.csv("benchmark-lowlabel.csv")
unsupervised_effects <- read.csv("benchmark-umap-hdbscan-effects.csv")
bertopic_seeds <- read.csv("benchmark-bertopic-seeds.csv")
bertopic_effects <- read.csv("benchmark-bertopic-effects.csv")

result_of <- function(data, m, column = "accuracy") {
  subset(results, dataset == data & method == m)[[column]]
}
fmt <- function(x) sprintf("%.4f", x)
pub <- function(data, m) fmt(subset(published, dataset == data & model == m)$accuracy)
low_at <- function(data, frac, m) {
  rows <- lowlabel[lowlabel$dataset == data & lowlabel$method == m, ]
  rows[abs(rows$fraction - frac) < 1e-9, ]
}
effect <- function(data, comp, metric, ref = NULL) {
  rows <- data[data$comparator == comp & data$metric == metric, ]
  if (!is.null(ref)) rows <- rows[rows$reference == ref, ]
  rows
}
largest <- subset(results, dataset == "20ng" & method == "hypergraph_zhou_cmn")
```

This article compares recorded results for hypergraph label spreading
on five text-classification datasets: R8, R52, MR, Ohsumed, and
20-Newsgroups. A tf-idf nearest-centroid classifier provides a baseline,
and published values from Ding et al. (2020) provide additional context.
Label spreading solves a regularised system of class scores rather than
training a neural network. It still requires choices about preprocessing,
the graph or hypergraph, the spreading coefficient, and the decision rule.

The tables are read from the accompanying benchmark CSV files. Knitting
this article formats those recorded results; it does not rerun the
benchmark fits. Accuracy is reported as a proportion, with higher values
indicating more correct test predictions. Published results and local
experiments are identified separately because their protocols differ.

## Setup

The local experiments use the corpus files and train/test splits of
Yao, Mao, and Luo (2019), also used by Ding et al. (2020). Each corpus
is represented as a sparse document–word hypergraph. Document nodes
include both training and test documents; only training labels are
provided to the spreading calculation. This is a transductive protocol,
in which test-document features are available during construction.
The sparse implementation solves one regularised linear system per
class using conjugate gradients.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
hg <- text_hypergraph(docs, weight = "tfidf", sparse = TRUE)
fit <- hg_classify(hg, labels = train_labels, normalization = "class_mass")
```

The recorded train/test counts match the reference splits. Word
hyperedge counts are
`r format(result_of("R8", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn", "n_edges"), big.mark = ",")`
for R8 and
`r format(result_of("R52", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn", "n_edges"), big.mark = ",")`
for R52. For MR, Ohsumed, and 20NG, the local vocabulary counts are
`r format(result_of("mr", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn", "n_edges"), big.mark = ",")`,
`r format(result_of("ohsumed", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn", "n_edges"), big.mark = ",")`,
and `r format(result_of("20ng", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn", "n_edges"), big.mark = ",")`,
compared with the published counts of 18,764, 14,157, and 42,757.
Tokenisation differs, including its treatment of digits. The recorded
MR construction also excludes one disconnected training document.
These differences limit exact comparability even when split identifiers
are shared.

## Full-split results

The table reports test accuracy, macro-averaged F1, construction
time (`build_s`), and classification time (`fit_s`). The accuracy interval
uses 1,000 bootstrap resamples of test predictions for a fixed fitted
solution. It describes resampling variation within that evaluation set,
not uncertainty from choosing another training split or model specification.

```{r}
knitr::kable(
  subset(results,
         select = c(dataset, method, accuracy, ci_low, ci_high, macro_f1,
                    build_s, fit_s)),
  digits = 4
)
```

For these recorded splits, class-mass-normalised Zhou label spreading
has accuracy `r fmt(result_of("20ng", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn"))` on 20NG
and `r fmt(result_of("mr", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn"))` on MR, compared with
`r fmt(result_of("20ng", "tfidf_centroid"))` and
`r fmt(result_of("mr", "tfidf_centroid"))` for the centroid baseline.
On R8, R52, and Ohsumed, the centroid baseline is more accurate in this
comparison. On R52, for example, the corresponding values are
`r fmt(result_of("R52", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn"))` and
`r fmt(result_of("R52", "tfidf_centroid"))`.
The datasets differ in vocabulary and class distribution as well as
size, so these comparisons do not isolate an effect of class imbalance.

Rows named `hypergraph_zhou` use the largest raw spreading score
without class-mass normalisation. Their accuracies are
`r fmt(result_of("R8", "hypergraph_zhou"))` on R8 and
`r fmt(result_of("20ng", "hypergraph_zhou"))` on 20NG.
The `cmn` suffix identifies the alternative decision rule, which
normalises each class-score column by its total mass before choosing
the largest score (Zhu et al. 2003). This changes the predictions
without changing the underlying linear solve.

`hypergraph_random_walk_cmn` instead uses the weighted random-walk
Laplacian (Chitra and Raphael 2019; Hayashi et al. 2020). On Ohsumed its
accuracy is
`r fmt(result_of("ohsumed", "hypergraph_random_walk_cmn"))`, compared with
`r fmt(result_of("ohsumed", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn"))` for the normalised
Zhou variant. This is a within-dataset comparison of two specified
operators, rather than a general ranking of Laplacian methods.

The largest recorded solve uses
`r format(largest$n_nodes, big.mark = ",")` documents,
`r format(largest$n_edges, big.mark = ",")` word hyperedges, and 20
classes. Its recorded classification time is
`r sprintf("%.1f", largest$fit_s)` seconds on the benchmark machine.
Runtime depends on hardware, matrix sparsity, solver tolerances, and
whether construction is included. These times are not a controlled
hardware comparison with the published neural models.

## Comparison with published results

The published table quotes means over ten runs from Table 2 of
Ding et al. (2020). The local spreading scores are deterministic
conditional on the corpus representation, labelled split, and solver
settings. Comparisons with inductive models have different information
conditions because the local hypergraph uses the features of the test
documents during construction.

```{r}
knitr::kable(published, digits = 4)
```

On 20NG, local Zhou label spreading has accuracy
`r fmt(result_of("20ng", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn"))`, compared with the
quoted values `r pub("20ng", "TextGCN (transductive)")` for transductive
TextGCN and `r pub("20ng", "HyperGAT")` for HyperGAT.
On MR, the corresponding values are
`r fmt(result_of("mr", "hypergraph_zhou_cmn"))`,
`r pub("mr", "TextGCN (transductive)")`, and
`r pub("mr", "HyperGAT")`. Read the remaining datasets from the table.
These results provide numerical context for a simple baseline; their
different preprocessing, training, and evaluation protocols preclude
attributing the differences to architecture alone.

## Few labels

The low-label experiment subsamples the training labels within
classes, retaining at least one seed per class. Both local methods
receive the same selected labels. Five draws are used at each fraction,
and `sd` reports the standard deviation across those draws. The graph
still includes unlabelled test-document features, so the experiment
remains transductive.

```{r}
knitr::kable(lowlabel, digits = 4)
```

On MR, the recorded 1% condition uses
`r low_at("mr", 0.01, "hypergraph_zhou_cmn")$n_seeds` labels and gives
accuracies
`r fmt(low_at("mr", 0.01, "hypergraph_zhou_cmn")$accuracy)` for spreading
and `r fmt(low_at("mr", 0.01, "tfidf_centroid")$accuracy)` for the
centroid. At 20%, the seed count is
`r format(low_at("mr", 0.2, "hypergraph_zhou_cmn")$n_seeds, big.mark = ",")`
and the accuracies are
`r fmt(low_at("mr", 0.2, "hypergraph_zhou_cmn")$accuracy)` and
`r fmt(low_at("mr", 0.2, "tfidf_centroid")$accuracy)`.
Inspect the table for the R8 and Ohsumed comparisons. Five draws
provide only a limited description of sensitivity to label selection;
they do not establish performance under other sampling mechanisms.

## Unsupervised clustering against UMAP and HDBSCAN

The clustering comparison fits R8 without using the document labels
as training inputs. Hypergraph spectral clustering requests eight
clusters. The alternatives use tf-idf features reduced by singular-value
decomposition and UMAP, followed by HDBSCAN or eight-cluster k-means.
The specified cluster count matches R8's eight reference classes, which
is information used in the comparison design.

Evaluate the resulting partitions using adjusted Rand index (ARI),
adjusted mutual information (AMI), and normalised mutual information
(NMI). The first two include a chance adjustment. All three measure
agreement with the reference labels, rather than intrinsic semantic
quality. This experiment uses the stated clustering pipeline rather
than the BERTopic package.

```{r}
knitr::kable(
  subset(unsupervised_effects,
         select = c(comparator, metric, hypergraphs_mean, baseline_mean,
                    mean_difference, difference_ci_low,
                    difference_ci_high, paired_dz)),
  digits = 4
)
```

The recorded HDBSCAN pipeline produces more than eight groups and
marks some documents as outliers. Its lower agreement with the reference
labels therefore combines differences in resolution, outlier handling,
and assignment. Against eight-cluster k-means, the mean ARI difference
favouring the hypergraph solution is
`r fmt(effect(unsupervised_effects, "umap_kmeans_k8", "ari")$mean_difference)`,
with paired bootstrap interval
`r fmt(effect(unsupervised_effects, "umap_kmeans_k8", "ari")$difference_ci_low)`
to `r fmt(effect(unsupervised_effects, "umap_kmeans_k8", "ari")$difference_ci_high)`.
The AMI and NMI differences have the opposite direction in the recorded
results. Report all selected metrics rather than treating one as a
complete ranking of the methods.

## BERTopic

A separate R8 experiment uses BERTopic 0.17.4 (Grootendorst 2022)
with `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` document embeddings, UMAP, HDBSCAN, and class-based
tf-idf. Ten seeds are recorded. The comparison includes the default
clustering, a model reduced to eight topics, and a reduced model with
outliers reassigned by embedding similarity.

Two hypergraph variants request eight clusters: a document–word tf-idf
hypergraph and a document kNN hypergraph constructed from the same
MiniLM embeddings. The embedding comparison holds the encoder output
fixed while changing neighbourhood construction and clustering.
This does not hold every downstream hyperparameter fixed.

```{r}
knitr::kable(
  aggregate(cbind(ari, ami, nmi, n_clusters, outlier_fraction) ~ method,
            data = bertopic_seeds, FUN = mean),
  digits = 4, caption = "Means over ten seeds"
)
knitr::kable(
  subset(bertopic_effects, comparator == "bertopic_k_assigned",
         select = c(reference, metric, hypergraphs_mean, baseline_mean,
                    mean_difference, difference_ci_low,
                    difference_ci_high)),
  digits = 4, caption = "Paired effects against the fully assigned eight-topic BERTopic"
)
```

```{r bertopic-values, include = FALSE}
shipped <- subset(bertopic_seeds, method == "bertopic_default")
tfidf_ari <- effect(bertopic_effects, "bertopic_k_assigned", "ari",
                    "hypergraphs_hypergraph")
knn_ari <- effect(bertopic_effects, "bertopic_k_assigned", "ari",
                  "hypergraphs_knn_sbert")
knn_ami <- effect(bertopic_effects, "bertopic_k_assigned", "ami",
                  "hypergraphs_knn_sbert")
```

Default BERTopic produces between `r min(shipped$n_clusters)` and
`r max(shipped$n_clusters)` topics and leaves an average of
`r round(100 * mean(shipped$outlier_fraction))`% of documents labelled
as outliers. Differences from the fully assigned eight-cluster solutions
therefore include both resolution and outlier treatment.

Against the eight-topic BERTopic variant with reassigned outliers, the
mean ARI differences are `r fmt(tfidf_ari$mean_difference)` for the
tf-idf hypergraph and `r fmt(knn_ari$mean_difference)` for the embedding
kNN hypergraph. Their paired intervals are
`r fmt(tfidf_ari$difference_ci_low)` to
`r fmt(tfidf_ari$difference_ci_high)` and
`r fmt(knn_ari$difference_ci_low)` to
`r fmt(knn_ari$difference_ci_high)`, respectively. The kNN AMI difference
is `r fmt(knn_ami$mean_difference)`.

These intervals summarise seed variation in the recorded runs. They
exclude uncertainty from corpus selection, encoder choice, and
hyperparameter selection. Only document assignments are evaluated;
BERTopic's topic representations are outside this comparison.

## Choice of method

Use these results to define comparisons for the intended application.
Include a transparent baseline, state whether the protocol is
transductive or inductive, and distinguish preprocessing from the
classification or clustering method. Compare decision rules on the
same split and report macro-F1 alongside accuracy when class balance
matters.

The recorded results support dataset-specific comparisons under the
reported settings. They do not establish that one method is generally
preferable for balanced, imbalanced, or sparsely labelled corpora.
For a new study, evaluate on held-out data and assess sensitivity to
label selection and model specification.
